nodes.label: Achaemenid Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The Persian province Alexander took: the temples and their archives and observatory still running, the chancery in Aramaic, the taxed satrapy, the Judean diaspora two centuries settled, and the astronomy already mature. See mesopotamia-539bc-331bc.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-539bc-331bc.

nodes.label: Parthian Mesopotamia
nodes.full: The Arsacid empire that took Seleucia in 141 and held the basin for three and a half centuries — keeping the Greek city, the temple science and the Seleucid administrative apparatus almost unchanged, and dating by 'Arsaces the king'. See mesopotamia-141bc-224.
nodes.src: background — see the folio mesopotamia-141bc-224.

nodes.label: Ptolemaic Egypt
nodes.full: The rival kingdom of Alexander's other great successor — Alexandria and its Library, Manetho writing Egypt's history in Greek, the Syrian Wars fought against the Seleucids for a century, and the large Greek-speaking Jewish community of the Nile.
nodes.src: background — see the folio egypt-332bc-30bc.

nodes.label: Antioch and the Seleucid west
nodes.full: Where the king actually lived, on the far side of the Syrian desert — the Mediterranean face of the empire, the ruler cult and the Greek gods, and the front on which the dynasty collided with Rome and lost.
nodes.src: background — Paul Kosmin, 'The Land of the Elephant Kings' (2014).

nodes.label: The Greek scientific world
nodes.full: Hipparchus and his successors, the island of Kos, the astronomers and astrologers who took over the Babylonian zodiac, the sexagesimal degree, the eclipse records and the birth-horoscope and carried them into the Western tradition for good.
nodes.src: background — Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975).

nodes.label: Seleucus I — the satrap who won a kingdom
nodes.full: Seleucus was given the satrapy of Babylon in the carve-up of 320, driven out by Antigonus in 315, and came back with a small force on a day the Babylonians long remembered — the first year of what became the Seleucid Era. He held the province through a hard four-year war, took the title of king around 305, ceded the far eastern lands to Chandragupta for five hundred war-elephants, and by his murder in 281 ruled from the Aegean to the Hindu Kush.
nodes.src: The Chronicle of the Diadochi (BCHP 3); Appian, 'Syriaca' 54–57; Diodorus Siculus XIX.90–92 on the return of 311.

nodes.label: Antiochus I — the restorer of the temples
nodes.full: Antiochus had governed the eastern half of the empire from Babylon as his father's co-king for fifteen years before he inherited it. In 268 he laid the foundations of Ezida at Borsippa in person and had the act recorded on a clay cylinder in Akkadian, in the old royal style — the last document of its kind. He also founded and settled Greek cities, and fought a long war to hold Syria against the Ptolemies.
nodes.src: The Antiochus Cylinder (Borsippa, 268 BC); Paul-Alain Beaulieu in 'The Oxford Handbook of Cuneiform Culture' (2011).

nodes.label: Antiochus II and Seleucus II — the middle reigns
nodes.full: Under Antiochus II and his son Seleucus II the dynasty turned on itself. A disputed marriage set off the Third Syrian War in 246: Ptolemy III's army marched up the Euphrates and into Babylon, and for a year the city was fought over street by street while a Seleucid garrison held the citadel. Seleucus II recovered the province but never the initiative, and lost the far east to the Parthians and Bactrians.
nodes.src: The Ptolemy III Chronicle (BCHP 11); Justin, 'Epitome' XXVII; the 'Gurob papyrus' on the Egyptian march.

nodes.label: Antiochus III the Great — the march east and the Roman check
nodes.full: Antiochus III put down a revolt that had seized Seleucia, then spent seven years marching to Bactria and India and back, recovering the appearance of empire. He turned west, collided with Rome, and was beaten at Magnesia in 190; the Treaty of Apamea took Anatolia and imposed a crushing indemnity. He died in 187 trying to plunder a temple in Elymais to help pay it.
nodes.src: Polybius V.40–56 (Molon) and XXI (Apamea); Diodorus XXVIII–XXIX; the death in Elymais in Strabo XVI.1.18.

nodes.label: Antiochus IV Epiphanes — the Greek city in Babylon
nodes.full: Antiochus IV gave Babylon a Greek constitution — a citizen body, a council, magistrates and a theatre — turning the old temple-city into a self-governing polis alongside its priesthood. The same policy of forced Hellenisation in Jerusalem produced the Maccabean revolt. He died in 164 on campaign in the Iranian highlands; a Babylonian record notes the news reaching the city.
nodes.src: The Astronomical Diaries for 175–164 BC (Sachs & Hunger); the Babylonian King List of the Hellenistic Period; 1 Maccabees 1; 6.

nodes.label: The last Seleucid decades and the loss of the land
nodes.full: After Antiochus IV the dynasty spent itself in succession wars fought in Syria, and Babylonia was governed at a distance by strategoi who could expect little help. When the Parthian king Mithridates I came down the Tigris in 141 there was no field army to stop him. Demetrius II marched east to recover the province in 138, was defeated and taken prisoner, and spent ten years as an Arsacid son-in-law.
nodes.src: The Astronomical Diary for 141 BC, which dates by 'Arsaces the king'; Justin XXXVI.1 and XXXVIII.9; Josephus, 'Antiquities' XIII.

nodes.label: The satrap, the strategos and the royal city
nodes.full: Babylonia was run for the king by a satrap, later titled strategos, seated at Seleucia — the eastern half of the empire's administrative capital, where the mint struck and the tribute was gathered. Below him a network of officers, most with Greek titles, oversaw the districts, the garrisons and the royal land. The king himself was normally at Antioch, on the far side of the Syrian desert.
nodes.src: Getzel Cohen, 'The Hellenistic Settlements in the East' (2013); Laurent Capdetrey, 'Le pouvoir séleucide' (2007).

nodes.label: The citizen body and the temple assembly
nodes.full: In the old cities the crown left the running of civic life to two bodies: the temple assembly — the šatammu of the Esagila and the kiništu council of priests and prebend-holders — and, in Babylon after Antiochus IV, a Greek-style citizen corporation, the politai, who appear in the Astronomical Diaries under an Akkadian version of the word. A royal overseer sat above both.
nodes.src: R. J. van der Spek, 'The Hellenistic Diaries and the Political History of Babylon' (2000); the puliṭē / politai in the Diaries.

nodes.label: The Babylonian War and the devastation of the land
nodes.full: When Seleucus came back in 311, Antigonus sent first his son Demetrius and then his whole army to take the province from him. The fighting ran for two years across the countryside; a Babylonian chronicle records 'weeping and mourning in the land', crops burnt and cities plundered, before Seleucus won a night battle and Antigonus withdrew for good. It fixed Babylonia as Seleucid.
nodes.src: The Chronicle of the Diadochi (BCHP 3); Diodorus Siculus XIX.100.

nodes.label: Ipsus and the ownership of the east
nodes.full: The four other successors combined against Antigonus and destroyed him at Ipsus in Phrygia in 301; Seleucus's Indian elephants decided the day. The battle was fought a thousand kilometres away, but it settled that Babylonia and the whole Asian core would be ruled from a single Seleucid throne rather than contested between warlords — the political fact that made Seleucia possible.
nodes.src: Plutarch, 'Demetrius' 28–29; Diodorus XXI.1.

nodes.label: The Ptolemaic army in Babylon
nodes.full: In the Third Syrian War Ptolemy III drove up through Syria and into Mesopotamia. A Babylonian chronicle records his troops fighting inside Babylon in 245, people killed in the streets, and a Seleucid garrison holding out in the royal fortress until relief came. It was the deepest a Ptolemaic army ever reached, and the last time Egypt threatened the Seleucid heartland.
nodes.src: The Ptolemy III Chronicle (BCHP 11); the 'Adulis inscription' (OGIS 54) for the Egyptian account.

nodes.label: The revolt of Molon at Seleucia
nodes.full: Molon, satrap of Media, rebelled against the young Antiochus III, crossed the Tigris, took Seleucia and the lowland cities, and struck his own royal coinage. Antiochus came east in person, caught Molon's army near the river, and won when part of it changed sides; Molon killed himself and his body was displayed. The king then crossed into Babylonia and sacrificed at the Esagila.
nodes.src: Polybius V.40–54.

nodes.label: The anabasis and the Roman indemnity
nodes.full: Antiochus III's seven-year march recovered tribute and treaties from Armenia to India and won him the title 'the Great'. Then Rome broke him at Magnesia in 190 and the Treaty of Apamea in 188 stripped Anatolia and imposed fifteen thousand talents of silver. The debt sent him and later his son to rob the temples of the eastern hills, where he was killed in 187.
nodes.src: Polybius XXI.42–45 (Apamea); Livy XXXVII–XXXVIII; Strabo XVI.1.18.

nodes.label: Mithridates I takes Babylonia
nodes.full: The Parthian king Mithridates I came down from Media and entered Seleucia in 141; within months the Diaries were dating documents by 'Arsaces the king'. Demetrius II's counter-attack in 138 ended in his capture. A last Seleucid effort under Antiochus VII briefly retook the land in 130 and collapsed when he was killed in battle in 129. After that Babylonia was Parthian for good.
nodes.src: The Astronomical Diaries for 141 and 130–129 BC; Justin XXXVI.1, XXXVIII.9–10, XLII.1.

nodes.label: The Seleucid Era — the first unbroken count of years
nodes.full: Seleucid scribes began numbering years continuously from Seleucus's return — year 1, year 2, on and on, with no restart at each new king. It was the first calendar era in history in the modern sense, and it stuck: the cuneiform tablets, then the Aramaic, Greek and much later Syriac and Arabic records of the Near East counted by it for more than a thousand years. The idea of a fixed epoch begins here.
nodes.src: Paul Kosmin, 'Time and Its Adversaries in the Seleucid Empire' (2018); the double-dated Babylonian tablets.

nodes.label: The constitution of Seleucia-on-the-Tigris
nodes.full: Seleucia was a full Greek polis dropped onto the Tigris: a citizen assembly, an elected council of three hundred, annual magistrates, Greek law, and a body of elders the sources call the peliganes. It was also the royal government's eastern seat. A city of Macedonians, Greeks, Babylonians, Syrians and Jews, it kept its civic machinery running under the Parthians and was still described as self-governing three centuries later.
nodes.src: Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.42; Getzel Cohen, 'The Hellenistic Settlements in the East' (2013).

nodes.label: Babylon made a polis
nodes.full: Antiochus IV planted a Greek citizen corporation inside Babylon — the politai, with their own officers, a gymnasium and a stone theatre built into the mound of the old New Year temple. The city now had two publics: the 'Babylonians' of the temple and the 'citizens' of the polis, sometimes acting together in the Diaries, sometimes at odds. It was Hellenisation by institution rather than by force.
nodes.src: R. J. van der Spek, 'The Hellenistic Diaries and the Political History of Babylon' (2000); the theatre excavated by the German expedition.

nodes.label: The temple assembly left to govern itself
nodes.full: The crown left the internal life of the old cities to the temple: the šatammu who administered the Esagila and the kiništu, the council of priests and prebend-holders. This assembly held land, ran courts, allocated the temple offices, kept the archives and the observatory, and issued its own decrees. It is the institution through which almost everything we know of Hellenistic Babylon was written down.
nodes.src: Gilles Boiy, 'Late Achaemenid and Hellenistic Babylon' (2004).

nodes.label: The royal land and the military settlers
nodes.full: Around the new cities the crown settled Greek and Macedonian soldiers on allotments — kleroi — held in return for service, a system carried over from the Achaemenid bow-land and given a Greek name. Beyond them stretched the 'royal land', worked by dependent villagers and sometimes granted to a queen or a favourite: a cuneiform deed records Antiochus II selling a huge estate to his former wife Laodice in 254.
nodes.src: The Laodice land sale (CT 49 = 'the Lehmann text'); G. G. Aperghis, 'The Seleukid Royal Economy' (2004).

nodes.label: The royal overseer above the priesthood
nodes.full: A royal official — an epistates, in the Diaries 'the man appointed over the temples' — sat above the temple assembly, controlling its money, confirming its officers, and forwarding the king's demands. The temples paid a levy on their income and their prebends. The relationship was the Achaemenid one continued: the old institutions kept running, under a hand that could reach into their treasury.
nodes.src: R. J. van der Spek, 'Multi-ethnicity and Ethnic Segregation in Hellenistic Babylon' (2009); the zazakku / epistates in the Diaries.

nodes.label: Marduk and the New Year still kept
nodes.full: Through the Seleucid century the Esagila kept its full ritual calendar. The Astronomical Diaries record the akitu procession down the sacred way, the offerings, and — when a king or his deputy was present — the rite of 'taking the hand of Bel' that made him legitimate in Babylon. Antiochus III performed it after defeating Molon. The cult of Marduk outlived the dynasty by two centuries.
nodes.src: The Astronomical Diaries (Sachs & Hunger); Julye Bidmead, 'The Akitu Festival' (2002).

nodes.label: The Astronomical Diaries at their fullest
nodes.full: The nightly record kept by the Esagila scholars reached its densest and most complete form in these decades: the positions of the moon and planets, eclipses, weather, river levels, commodity prices, and the news of the day, month after month without a break. It is the longest continuous scientific archive of the ancient world, and the raw material of the mathematical astronomy built on top of it.
nodes.src: A. J. Sachs & H. Hunger, 'Astronomical Diaries and Related Texts from Babylonia' (1988–2006).

nodes.label: The rebuilding of the Uruk temples
nodes.full: Uruk in the third century rebuilt its sanctuaries on a scale never seen before: the vast Bit Resh of Anu and Antu and the Irigal of Ishtar, raised by the city governors Anu-uballit-Nikarchos and Anu-uballit-Kephalon, each of whom carried a Greek name beside his Babylonian one. Anu was promoted to head of the pantheon, and the old scholar families — the heirs of Sin-leqi-unninni — ran the cult and its learning.
nodes.src: The Anu-uballit building inscriptions (SE 68 and 110); Paul-Alain Beaulieu, 'The Cult of AN in Hellenistic Uruk' (1992).

nodes.label: The Jewish community of Babylonia continues
nodes.full: The Judean population that had chosen to stay under the Persians farmed, traded and worshipped through the Seleucid period as a settled, largely self-governing community, in contact with Jerusalem but distinct from it. The evidence is thin for these two centuries, but the institutions that later made Babylonia the world centre of Jewish learning — the exilarch, the academies — grew from this unbroken presence.
nodes.src: Josephus, 'Antiquities' XI–XII; Isaiah Gafni, 'The Jews of Babylonia in the Talmudic Era' (1990).

nodes.label: Greek gods and the cult of the king
nodes.full: The new cities worshipped Apollo, claimed as the dynasty's divine ancestor, and Zeus, and honoured the living king and his dead predecessors with civic cult and priesthoods. Greeks equated Bel with Zeus and Nabu with Apollo, and the two religious worlds ran side by side without merging: the Babylonian temple kept its rites, the polis kept its altars, and few people crossed between them.
nodes.src: The Seleucid ruler cult in the 'Sardis' and 'Nihavand' inscriptions (OGIS 224, 231); interpretatio in Berossus.

nodes.label: Berossus explains Babylon to the Greeks
nodes.full: A priest of Bel named Berossus wrote a history of Babylonia in Greek and dedicated it to Antiochus I: the fish-man Oannes bringing civilisation, the ten kings before the flood, the flood itself, and the dynasties down to Alexander, drawn from cuneiform sources. It was the first time the Babylonian account of the world was put into a language the wider Mediterranean could read.
nodes.src: Berossus, 'Babyloniaca', frags. in Gerald Verbrugghe & John Wickersham, 'Berossos and Manetho' (1996).

nodes.label: The Antiochus Cylinder — the last royal inscription in Akkadian
nodes.full: To mark his rebuilding of Ezida, Antiochus I had a clay barrel-cylinder inscribed in Akkadian, in deliberately archaic language, styling him 'king of the world, king of Babylon, king of the lands', provider for Esagila and Ezida, in the exact form Nebuchadnezzar had used. It is the last building inscription any king wrote in the Babylonian language and script — a two-thousand-year royal tradition ending on a single object.
nodes.src: The Antiochus Cylinder (BM 36277); Kathryn Stevens, 'The Antiochus Cylinder, Babylonian Scholarship and Seleucid Imperial Ideology' (JHS 2014).

nodes.label: The last copying of the classics
nodes.full: The temple schools of Babylon and Uruk went on copying the old library — the Epic of Creation, Gilgamesh, the omen series, the lexical lists, the hymns — with dated colophons naming the young scribes and their teachers. The readership was now a few dozen families of priests. When the copying stopped, in the first century, a written literature that had run since the third millennium simply ended.
nodes.src: Philippe Clancier, 'Les bibliothèques en Babylonie dans la seconde moitié du Ier millénaire av. J.-C.' (2009).

nodes.label: The Graeco-Babyloniaca tablets
nodes.full: A small group of clay tablets carries Sumerian and Akkadian text on one face and a transliteration into Greek letters on the other — school exercises made by scribes who could still read cuneiform but now thought in the Greek alphabet. They are the fossil of the changeover: the last generations for whom the wedge-script was a living skill, learning it through the writing that was replacing it.
nodes.src: Mark Geller, 'The Last Wedge' (ZA 1997); the Graeco-Babyloniaca corpus.

nodes.label: The Hellenistic chronicles on clay
nodes.full: The Esagila scholars kept writing history in the old form — terse Akkadian chronicles on clay tablets, recording the campaigns of the successors, the Ptolemaic invasion, the arrival of elephants, the acts of the kings in Babylon. Compiled from the daily Diaries, they are the only contemporary narrative of Seleucid Mesopotamia written from inside it rather than by a distant Greek.
nodes.src: I. Finkel, R. J. van der Spek & R. Pirngruber, 'Babylonian Chronographic Texts from the Hellenistic Period' (BCHP).

nodes.label: The theatre and the sealed archive
nodes.full: The new idiom was Greek and civic: a stone theatre raised on the mound of Babylon's New Year temple, terracotta figurines of Greek types turned out by the thousand, and at Seleucia an archive whose clay sealings — some thirty thousand of them, stamped with Greek gods, portraits and civic emblems — survived a fire that destroyed the papyri they had closed.
nodes.src: Antonio Invernizzi, 'Seleucia on the Tigris: the sealings' (2004); the Babylon theatre in the German excavation reports.

nodes.label: Systems A and B — astronomy by arithmetic
nodes.full: Babylonian astronomers built two complete arithmetical schemes — modern scholars call them System A and System B — that could compute the position of the moon or a planet, the length of the month, and the time of an eclipse for any date, years in advance, using only tables of numbers and step-by-step rules. No geometry, no model of the heavens: pure calculation, and accurate to minutes.
nodes.src: Otto Neugebauer, 'Astronomical Cuneiform Texts' (1955); Mathieu Ossendrijver, 'Babylonian Mathematical Astronomy: Procedure Texts' (2012).

nodes.label: The Goal-Year method of prediction
nodes.full: For a quicker forecast the scholars used period relations — the eighteen-year eclipse cycle, the eight-year return of Venus, the seventy-one-year cycle of Jupiter — pulling the record from that many years back and adjusting it. The 'Goal-Year Texts' collected exactly the old data needed to predict the coming year. It is empirical prediction from a long archive, the method modern astronomy was still using centuries later.
nodes.src: John Steele & others, 'Goal-Year Astronomy in Babylon' (2019); Hermann Hunger, 'Goal-Year texts' in the ADRT series.

nodes.label: Seleucus of Seleucia argues the earth moves
nodes.full: An astronomer from Seleucia — writing in Greek, trained in the Babylonian tradition — is the only thinker in antiquity known to have positively argued that Aristarchus was right and the earth turns and circles the sun, not merely floated it as a hypothesis. He also connected the tides to the moon's motion and tried to explain their monthly variation. Almost none of his work survives.
nodes.src: Plutarch, 'Platonic Questions' 1006c and 'On the Face in the Moon' 923a; Strabo I.1.9, III.5.9, XVI.1.6.

nodes.label: The horoscope comes of age
nodes.full: The oldest surviving birth-charts — the positions of the sun, moon and planets in the zodiac at a named child's birth, with a reading of the life to come — are Babylonian, and the genre matured in the Seleucid period. It fused the mathematical astronomy that could compute those positions with the old omen tradition, and it is the direct ancestor of every horoscope cast since.
nodes.src: Francesca Rochberg, 'Babylonian Horoscopes' (1998).

nodes.label: The parameters pass to Hipparchus
nodes.full: Around 140 BC the Greek astronomer Hipparchus was working with Babylonian eclipse records going back four centuries, Babylonian values for the length of the month and the year, the division of the circle into 360 degrees, and the sexagesimal fractions — the whole quantitative apparatus of Greek astronomy from Hipparchus to Ptolemy rests on a Mesopotamian foundation laid in these centuries.
nodes.src: G. J. Toomer, 'Hipparchus and Babylonian Astronomy' (1988); Alexander Jones, 'The Adaptation of Babylonian Methods in Greek Numerical Astronomy' (1991).

nodes.label: Seleucia draws off Babylon's people
nodes.full: Seleucus built his eastern capital forty kilometres north of Babylon and moved population into it — Greek and Macedonian settlers, and, the Greek sources say, many Babylonians ordered to relocate. Within two generations Seleucia was one of the largest cities on earth and Babylon was visibly emptier: the Diaries record whole quarters abandoned and the built-up area shrinking back toward the temple.
nodes.src: Pliny, 'Natural History' VI.30.122; Pausanias I.16.3; the depopulation in the Astronomical Diaries.

nodes.label: The coined-silver economy arrives in earnest
nodes.full: The Seleucia mint was one of the busiest in the empire, striking Attic-weight silver tetradrachms and small bronze for everyday use. Coin now did much of the work that weighed silver had done, and the crown paid its soldiers and officials in it. Old habits held on — temple contracts still reckoned in silver 'by the shekel' — but the region had joined a monetised Mediterranean economy.
nodes.src: Arthur Houghton & Catharine Lorber, 'Seleucid Coins' (2002); G. G. Aperghis, 'The Seleukid Royal Economy' (2004).

nodes.label: The temple as landlord and bank
nodes.full: The Esagila held estates, date-groves, herds and workshops, rented them out, and lent silver at interest. Its offices were owned as property: a 'prebend' — the right to a share of the temple's income and offerings for so many days a year, attached to a task like baker, brewer or exorcist — was inherited, divided among heirs, mortgaged and sold, with its market price written into the deed.
nodes.src: Gilles Boiy, 'Late Achaemenid and Hellenistic Babylon' (2004); the prebend sales in the Esagila archive.

nodes.label: The four-century price record
nodes.full: Every month the Diaries noted how much barley, dates, mustard, cress, sesame and wool a shekel of silver would buy in Babylon. Kept up for more than three hundred years, it is by far the longest run of price data from the ancient world — enough to show the seasonal swing, the long inflation after Alexander, and the brutal spikes when war or a bad flood cut the harvest.
nodes.src: Alice Slotsky, 'The Bourse of Babylon' (1997); Reinhard Pirngruber, 'The Economy of Late Achaemenid and Seleucid Babylonia' (2017).

nodes.label: The Gulf route and the desert road
nodes.full: Seleucia sat where the river route down to the Persian Gulf — and on to Arabia and India — met the caravan road that crossed the Syrian desert to Antioch and the Mediterranean. Frankincense from South Arabia, pepper and cotton from India, textiles and slaves moved through it. The Arab merchant town of Gerrha on the Gulf coast grew rich as the sea leg's western terminal.
nodes.src: Strabo XVI.3–4; Raymond Descat & others on Hellenistic Gulf trade; the Gerrha references in Polybius XIII.9.

nodes.label: The king's demand on Babylonia
nodes.full: Babylonia remained one of the richest sources of Seleucid revenue: the land tax on grain and dates, the salt tax, the crown's own estates, tolls on the trade routes, and a levy on the temples' income and offices. Modern reconstructions of the Seleucid budget put the eastern satrapies, with Babylonia at their centre, among the largest single contributors to a treasury run from Syria.
nodes.src: G. G. Aperghis, 'The Seleukid Royal Economy' (2004); Makis Aperghis on temple taxation.

nodes.label: The grid plan of Seleucia
nodes.full: Seleucia was laid out in one operation on the Greek model — a rectangular grid of straight streets and standard blocks covering more than five square kilometres, a walled circuit, an agora, the royal quarter and a harbour cut on the Tigris. Italian excavation traced the block system across the whole site. It was city-building as an instrument of rule: a capital designed, not grown.
nodes.src: Antonio Invernizzi & others, 'Seleucia al Tigri' (excavation reports, 1967–1990).

nodes.label: The Royal Canal between the rivers
nodes.full: The Seleucids maintained and enlarged the great transverse canal — the Greeks called it the 'Royal River' — that ran from the Euphrates across to the Tigris at Seleucia, carrying barge traffic between the two rivers and watering the land between. It made the new capital a river port with access to both systems, and tied Seleucia's prosperity to the upkeep of the works.
nodes.src: Strabo XVI.1.9–11; Pliny VI.30; the Nahr Malka / Ar-Malik in the later Arab geographers.

nodes.label: Fired brick, mortar and the vault
nodes.full: Hellenistic builders in the alluvium — where stone had to be imported — worked in baked brick set in lime mortar, with rubble cores, barrel vaults and, at Seleucia, the peristyle courtyard house of the Greek world reproduced in mudbrick and plaster. The Babylon theatre combined a Greek plan with local brick construction. The materials were Mesopotamian; the forms were new.
nodes.src: the Seleucia housing blocks (Italian excavations); the Babylon theatre reports (Koldewey / Wetzel).

nodes.label: The drift of the Euphrates
nodes.full: The Euphrates was slowly abandoning its Babylon channel for a western course, and the diversion of water toward Seleucia and the marsh outlet at the Pallukkatu made it worse. Keeping enough flow in the old bed to water Babylon and turn its mills became a running problem the Diaries mention. The river that had made the city was leaving it.
nodes.src: the water-shortage notices in the Astronomical Diaries; Hermann Gasche & others on the Euphrates channel shifts.

nodes.label: Seleucia, the great emporium of the East
nodes.full: Seleucia was where the roads met: the desert crossing from Antioch and the Mediterranean, the highland routes into Iran and Central Asia, the river down to the Gulf and India, the caravan tracks from Arabia. Pliny called it the trade capital of the East. For four centuries — Seleucid then Parthian — it was the point through which the Mediterranean and the Asian worlds did business.
nodes.src: Pliny, 'Natural History' VI.30.122; Strabo XVI.1.5.

nodes.label: The treaty with Chandragupta and Megasthenes' embassy
nodes.full: Rather than fight the new Mauryan empire, Seleucus I gave up the eastern satrapies bordering India in exchange for five hundred war-elephants — the elephants that won Ipsus two years later — and a marriage tie. He sent Megasthenes as ambassador to Pataliputra, whose report, the 'Indika', was the Greek world's main account of India for centuries.
nodes.src: Strabo XV.2.9 and XVI.1.3; Appian, 'Syriaca' 55; the fragments of Megasthenes.

nodes.label: The Chaldeans as a profession abroad
nodes.full: 'Chaldean' became a Greek and then Roman word for an astronomer-astrologer, and the real thing travelled: the tradition that Berossus settled on Kos and taught there, the Babylonian parameters and eclipse records in Greek hands, the spread of the birth-horoscope across the Hellenistic world. The prestige of Babylonian sky-knowledge outlived the ability to read the tablets it came from.
nodes.src: Vitruvius IX.6.2 (Berossus on Kos); Otto Neugebauer, 'A History of Ancient Mathematical Astronomy' (1975).

nodes.label: The Gulf garrison on Ikaros
nodes.full: The Seleucids held the head of the Persian Gulf: a fort and a Greek temple to a saviour goddess on the island of Failaka — renamed Ikaros — with a Greek garrison, and influence on Bahrain, the Tylos of the Greeks. An inscription from the island preserves a royal officer's orders about its cults and settlers. It was the empire's watch on the sea route to India.
nodes.src: the 'Ikadion' / Ikaros inscription (SEG 35.1476); the Danish excavations on Failaka.

nodes.label: The Judaean tie and the coming crisis
nodes.full: When Antiochus III took Judaea from the Ptolemies in 200, the Jewish community of Babylonia and the homeland were under one crown for the first time in centuries. A generation later Antiochus IV's drive to make Jerusalem a Greek city — the same policy he applied to Babylon — set off the Maccabean revolt, and Babylonian Jewry became a place of support and refuge for it.
nodes.src: Josephus, 'Antiquities' XII.3; 1 and 2 Maccabees; Elias Bickerman, 'The God of the Maccabees' (1937).

nodes.label: Old Babylon and new Seleucia
nodes.full: For a century Mesopotamia had two great cities forty kilometres apart: Babylon, two millennia old, sacred, its temple still the centre of a learned world but its houses thinning; and Seleucia, built in a decade, secular, Greek-governed, and soon the larger by far. The centre of gravity of the land moved north from the one to the other, and never moved back.
nodes.src: Tom Boiy, 'Between High and Low: A Chronology of the Early Hellenistic Period' (2007); Pliny VI.30.

nodes.label: A Greek layer over an Aramaic land
nodes.full: The Greeks and Macedonians were a thin stratum — soldiers, officials, city-dwellers — spread over a population that spoke Aramaic, farmed as it always had, and prayed in the old temples. The evidence points more to two communities living side by side, each with its own law and institutions, than to a melting pot. A Babylonian might take a Greek name for business and stay wholly Babylonian at home.
nodes.src: R. J. van der Spek, 'Multi-ethnicity and Ethnic Segregation in Hellenistic Babylon' (2009).

nodes.label: The far eastern limit of the polis
nodes.full: Seleucia and its sister foundations mark about as far east as the self-governing Greek city reached and durably held. Beyond the Tigris the Greek presence was garrisons and trade posts in an Iranian world that stayed Iranian, and when the Parthians came the frontier of Hellenism fell back to roughly this line — where it had first been drawn by Alexander's colonists.
nodes.src: Frank Holt, 'Thundering Zeus: The Making of Hellenistic Bactria' (1999); Getzel Cohen (2013).

nodes.label: The Seleucid template
nodes.full: The Seleucid settlement of Mesopotamia was the Achaemenid one with a Greek layer added: a satrap for a distant king, tribute, the temples and their science left running — plus an era count, a chancery in Greek, and a scatter of self-governing cities. The Parthians took the whole apparatus over almost unchanged, Seleucia and all, and ran it for the next three and a half centuries.
nodes.src: Paul Kosmin, 'The Land of the Elephant Kings' (2014); Josef Wiesehöfer, 'Ancient Persia' (2001).

nodes.label: The astronomer-scribe of the Esagila
nodes.full: He held an astronomy prebend — a share of the temple's bread, dates and silver in return for the sky-watch — observed and wrote up the Diary night after night, computed the ephemeris tables from the arithmetical schemes, and taught the whole craft to his son. His family had done it for generations. He was the working edge of exact science and the last keeper of a script almost no one else could read.
nodes.src: the astronomers' archive and family names in Philippe Clancier (2009); Mathieu Ossendrijver (2012).

nodes.label: The Greek colonist on the Tigris
nodes.full: The grandson of a Macedonian veteran, he was a citizen of Seleucia — a vote in the assembly, an allotment of land held for military service, his sons in the gymnasium, his marriage within the Greek community. He would have called the place home and Babylon a curiosity down the river. His city kept its Greek constitution running long after the king who founded it was gone.
nodes.src: the civic institutions of Seleucia in Tacitus, 'Annals' VI.42; Getzel Cohen (2013).

nodes.label: The Babylonian priest-notable
nodes.full: A member of the kiništu, he held income-prebends in more than one temple, sat on the assembly that ran the city's affairs, and spoke for it before the royal overseer when the king's demands came down. He wore the linen of his office at the festivals, kept the old genealogies, and — like his colleagues — carried a Greek alias for the parts of life that now ran in Greek.
nodes.src: the double names and the assembly in R. J. van der Spek (2000, 2009).

nodes.label: Berossus, priest and Greek author
nodes.full: A priest of Bel who learned Greek, read the cuneiform record, and wrote Babylonia's history and cosmology for a Greek readership and a Seleucid king. The later tradition has him leaving for the island of Kos and teaching astronomy and astrology there until he died. Whether or not that is true, he stands for the priest who became the interpreter — the last insider who could still explain the tablets from within.
nodes.src: Berossus in Verbrugghe & Wickersham (1996); Vitruvius IX.6.2.

nodes.label: The bilingual scribe
nodes.full: He could write a barley lease in Akkadian on a clay tablet for the temple archive in the morning and a tax receipt in Greek on parchment for the royal office in the afternoon. His father had worked only in clay; his sons would work only in Greek and Aramaic. He belonged to the single generation that spanned the changeover, and the Graeco-Babyloniaca exercises are the trace it left.
nodes.src: Mark Geller, 'The Last Wedge' (ZA 1997).
